content.fullText:
[00:00] In this lecture, I will make a succinct review of the pitchfork and then I will introduce a few new ideas that come from the mixture of pitchforks, Fibonacci ratios and the idea of reversal fields.
[00:16] To draw a pitchfork, we need three anchor points. In the case of real anchor points, these three anchors must be alternating, meaning a low, a high and a low, or a high, a low and a high. In the case of abstract anchor points, this definition of alternating points is relaxed, as we saw in some of the lectures involving the pitchforks in the line theory.
[00:39] There are basically two main types of pitchfork: the standard and the modified Schiff. The standard is the most common where we simply ground the fork on three anchoring points. The modified Schiff is a derivation from the standard where the A-axis of the fork is moved to the midpoint of the AB segment. These are the two most common types of forks we'll use.
[01:04] Pitchforks also have auxiliary lines. We have the double lines and the parallel lines. A double line is simply a Newtonian extrapolation of the already existing action spaces of the pitchfork. A parallel line is simply an overthrow or underthrow line or a line that runs parallel to the main fork lines. Parallel lines tend to follow the third law of motion where an action has an equal and opposite reaction. For example, an overthrow in one of the fork lines can generate an underthrow in the other fork line.
[01:39] Another interesting application of parallel lines is that we can ground them on the original inward frequencies, especially those in the c-axis of a pitchfork. Lines like these can give very interesting entry points that can be difficult to see in other ways. In this image, we can see a standard pitchfork with a parallel line grounded on the inward frequency related to the market extreme where the c-axis of the pitchfork was grounded. Notice how the parallel line catches the next market edges.
[02:11] Advancing the techniques related to the pitchfork lines a little bit more, we can mix them with the well-known Fibonacci ratios to create what I call a Fibfork. Similarly to what we saw in the two types of action space extrapolations, instead of using Newtonian extrapolation as it is usually done with pitchforks, we can use Fibonacci ratios to create non-equidistant line extrapolations that follow the peculiar angle found by the pitchfork.
[02:40] In this image, we can see a Fibfork that uses a 61.8% parallel line. Notice how the Fibonacci-based parallel lines catch the future frequencies of price action. Fibonacci ratios related to a pitchfork tend to work quite well, and we can use these lines to advance the technique even more by using the idea of reversal fields.
[03:02] For example, when we have a Fibfork with a 61.8 parallel line, this line will create a sloped zone that follows the angle of the fork. When we have two Fibforks with sloped zones, we have areas in the chart where these sloped zones will intersect, creating a polygonal field of probable reversal. In this image, we can see a few Fibforks. The 61.8% parallel line and the outer lines of the fork form a sloped zone. The areas where the sloped zones of the Fibforks intersect, we have the creation of a polygonal field of probable reversal. Notice how price reverses as it enters the polygonal fields.
[03:47] It's important to remember that, technically speaking, we can use any Fibonacci ratio to create Fibforks of various kinds. But for the sake of simplicity, it's best to use only the most powerful ratios like 61.8% and the 161.8%. It's also important to remember that all these pitchfork techniques are interchangeable, meaning that we can use any type of fork with any type of auxiliary line and with any type of Fibonacci ratio.

keyEvents.description: Title slide with a white background. The text reads: 'Pitchforks, Inward Parallels, Fibforks & Polygonal Fields'. In the background is a faded white marble bust of a classical Greek philosopher, likely Aristotle.

A diagram appears illustrating a Standard Pitchfork. It shows three points labeled 'A-axis', 'B-axis', and 'C-axis' connected by lines, forming a zig-zag pattern. Three parallel blue lines are projected forward from these points, forming the pitchfork channel.

The diagram is updated to compare the 'Standard Pitchfork' (blue) with the 'Modified Schiff Pitchfork' (red). A new label, 'AB Midpoint', is shown halfway along the line connecting the A and B axes. The Modified Schiff Pitchfork originates from this midpoint instead of the A-axis.

A diagram shows a zig-zag price action path moving upwards within a standard pitchfork. An additional parallel line, equidistant to the upper pitchfork line, is added and labeled 'Double Line (Newtonian Extrapolation)', showing a potential target for a strong breakout.

The diagram is modified to illustrate overthrows and underthrows. Red parallel lines are drawn slightly outside the main blue pitchfork channel. The upper red line is labeled 'Overthrow' and the lower is labeled 'Underthrow'. The price path is shown temporarily exceeding the main channel to touch these outer lines before reversing.

A live forex candlestick chart (FX EUR/USD, 120min) is displayed. A standard blue pitchfork is drawn on the price action. A new parallel line, labeled 'The Inward Frequency Parallel Line', is drawn, starting from a low point before the pitchfork's C-axis. Green rectangles highlight subsequent price lows that precisely touch this line, acting as support. On-screen text explains the concept.

The candlestick chart now shows a 'Fibfork'. This is a standard pitchfork with additional parallel lines drawn based on Fibonacci ratios. The lines are labeled '61.8% Parallel'. Green rectangles highlight multiple price highs and lows that find resistance and support on these new Fibonacci-derived parallel lines.

The chart now illustrates 'Polygonal Fields'. Several intersecting pitchforks are drawn. The space between the outer fork line and the 61.8% parallel line is shaded, creating a 'sloped zone'. Where two of these sloped zones from different pitchforks intersect, they form a shaded rhombus shape labeled 'Polygonal Field'. Blue arrows point to market reversals occurring precisely within these polygonal intersection zones.

semanticAnalysis.mainConcept: The core concept is the systematic advancement of the Andrews Pitchfork as a technical analysis tool. The lecture progresses from the basic Standard and Modified Schiff pitchforks to more complex applications by incorporating auxiliary lines (Double Lines, Over/Underthrow Parallels). It then introduces two novel concepts: 1) 'Inward Parallels,' which are grounded on prior market frequencies to project future support/resistance, and 2) 'Fibforks,' which integrate Fibonacci ratios (specifically 61.8%) to create non-equidistant, harmonically significant parallel lines. The final and most advanced technique is the creation of 'Polygonal Fields,' which are high-probability reversal zones identified by the intersection of 'sloped zones' from multiple Fibforks.
semanticAnalysis.deeperMeaning: The lecture implies that market price action is not random but follows a predictable geometric and harmonic structure. By moving beyond simple equidistant channels, the methodology suggests that market dynamics—such as momentum (Newtonian extrapolation) and harmonic waves (Fibonacci ratios)—can be mapped onto a geometric framework. The concept of 'Polygonal Fields' represents a form of confluence, where the intersection of multiple geometric and proportional structures creates a localized area of high energy, leading to probable market reversals. This approach provides a sophisticated method for identifying dynamic, angled zones of support and resistance that are more adaptive to market flow than static horizontal levels.
semanticAnalysis.educationalGoal: The educational objective is to transition a trader from a basic understanding of pitchforks to an advanced, multi-layered analytical method. The video aims to equip traders with a specific, proprietary-feeling toolkit for framing price action and identifying high-probability turning points. It fits within a broader curriculum that emphasizes geometric charting, market structure, and the search for underlying order in seemingly chaotic markets. The progressive layering of concepts—from simple forks to Fibforks to Polygonal Fields—is designed to build a comprehensive and nuanced trading methodology based on the principles of action-reaction and harmonic proportions.
